topic: Compile-Time Polymorphism with `constexpr` and its Impact on Memory Layout and Performance
explanation: This concept explores how `constexpr` functions and variables enable compile-time computation, influencing memory layout and runtime performance.  We'll examine how compilers optimize `constexpr` code, potentially eliminating runtime overhead entirely and leading to significant performance gains. We will also discuss the limitations of `constexpr` and situations where compile-time evaluation might not be possible, focusing on the interaction between `constexpr` and external factors, such as I/O or dynamic memory allocation.
example_explanation: The `constexpr` fibonacci function demonstrates compile-time computation.  In the `main` function, `fib_sequence` is initialized with the results of `fibonacci` calls at compile time. The compiler directly substitutes the calculated values into the array, avoiding any runtime computation for accessing elements of `fib_sequence`. Accessing `fib_sequence[i]` will involve a simple array access at runtime.  Conversely, the call to `fibonacci(20)` occurs at runtime, resulting in recursive function calls and the associated overhead.  The compiler's optimization will heavily favor the `constexpr` version, potentially reducing the compiled code size and improving execution speed. The difference becomes significant for larger values of `n`, where the runtime cost of the recursive calls in `fibonacci(20)` will be substantial.  Examining the assembly code would reveal the absence of function calls for accessing `fib_sequence` (it would be directly embedded in the code), while the `fibonacci(20)` call will translate into actual function calls and stack operations.  Note that the feasibility of compile-time evaluation is tightly coupled to the complexity of the `constexpr` function; excessively complex computations might exceed the compiler's capacity for compile-time resolution.
